chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Yaqteen, from Al-Fadl ibn Kathir Al-Madainy, from the one who mentioned it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

One of his companions entered upon him and saw upon him a shirt with a patch that had been sewn onto it, so he kept looking at it. Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him: 'What is the matter with you, that you are looking?' He said: 'A patch attached in your shirt.' He (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Strike your hand to this book and read what is in it.' And in front of him was a book, or near to him. So the man looked in it, and there was in it: 'There is no faith for the one who has no shame, nor any wealth for the one who has no esteem, nor anything new for the one who does not have (anything) old for him.'

key_terms.حَيَاءَ: Shame, modesty, or bashfulness; a key moral virtue in Islam.
key_terms.خَلَقَ: Antiquity, age, or being old/ancient; referring to the state of being worn or established.
key_terms.قَبٌّ: A patch or piece of cloth sewn onto a garment to mend a hole or wear.

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of the hadith about faith, shame, and patched clothes in Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: In this narrative from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) transforms a moment of social scrutiny over his patched garment into a profound lesson on *khuluq* (character) and *hayaa* (modesty/shame), core virtues in Shia ethics. By referencing a book containing the maxim 'There is no faith for one who has no modesty,' he highlights that inner spiritual integrity supersedes material wealth or novelty, a theme deeply resonant with the concept of *Zuhd* (asceticism) among the Imams. This incident underscores the scholarly view that true nobility is derived from moral conduct rather than external appearances.
